title: Chinese Mythology: Figures, Relationships and Story Cycles
description: The Chinese pantheon mapped as a relationship graph: Pangu and the making of the world, Nuwa and the mending of the sky, the sage kings, the celestial bureaucracy of the Jade Emperor, the Eight Immortals and the Journey to the West.
sources: E. T. C. Werner, Myths and Legends of China (1922)
John C. Ferguson, Chinese Mythology, Mythology of All Races VIII (1928)
James Legge, The Shu King (1879) and The Writings of Chuang Tzu (1891)
Timothy Richard, A Mission to Heaven (1913), a condensation of Journey to the West
Herbert A. Giles, Strange Stories from a Chinese Studio (1880)
Encyclopaedia Britannica and Wikipedia for cross-checking dates, texts and layers
portraitNote: Portraits are original illustrations in a single uniform style for the whole pack, stored locally in the portraits/chinese/ folder. No images are fetched from the network.

profile.cosmicNature: Cyclical and administrative. Pangu's body becomes the physical world, and thereafter time is measured in dynasties that rise and fall by the Mandate of Heaven, and in vast Buddhist-influenced kalpas. The world is not destroyed and remade in a single catastrophe; it is continually re-ordered, and disorder is a failure of administration rather than a war against chaos.
profile.natureOfDivinity: Bureaucratic and promotable. The celestial court mirrors the imperial one: gods hold ranks and offices, file reports, are appointed, promoted, censured and replaced. A mortal of exceptional merit can be enrolled as a god after death - Guan Yu, a Han general, ends up a major deity - and a god can be demoted for incompetence. This is the single most distinctive feature of the system.
profile.afterlife: Judicial and temporary. The dead pass through the ten courts of Diyu, where officials examine a record of their deeds, assign punishment in the appropriate department, and then return them to rebirth. It is processing rather than damnation: the sentence is served and the soul re-enters the cycle, and the whole apparatus is imagined as a very large and very thorough government office.
profile.systemMechanism: The Mandate of Heaven and the celestial bureaucracy. Heaven confers the right to rule on the virtuous and withdraws it from the corrupt, which makes rebellion legitimate once the mandate has visibly lapsed - floods, famines and portents are read as notice of withdrawal. Order is maintained by correct office-holding at every level, from the Jade Emperor down to the god of a single village's earth.
profile.canonTexts: The Shanhaijing (Classic of Mountains and Seas), the Huainanzi, the Chuci, the Shujing, the Daoist canon including the Zhuangzi, and the Ming vernacular novels Fengshen Yanyi and Journey to the West, which fixed much of the popular pantheon in the form it still has.

hierarchy.title: Before the Separation
hierarchy.blurb: A cosmic egg, a giant who holds heaven and earth apart until he dies of it, a woman with a serpent's body who makes people out of clay and later patches the broken sky with melted stone.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: The sky is propped, the people are made, and the world is set in order

hierarchy.title: The Sage Kings
hierarchy.blurb: Culture heroes and model rulers who invent agriculture, medicine, writing and flood control. Yao passes over his own son for a commoner, and that abdication becomes the founding argument that legitimacy rests on virtue.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Heaven confers the mandate on the virtuous and withdraws it from the corrupt

hierarchy.title: The Celestial Court
hierarchy.blurb: Heaven is a civil service. Gods hold ranks and offices, file reports, are promoted, censured and replaced, and the Jade Emperor governs through ministries that mirror the imperial ones exactly.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Mortals of merit are enrolled into it, and a stone monkey storms its gates

hierarchy.title: The Immortals
hierarchy.blurb: Transcendence is achievable. The Eight Immortals are a beggar, a cripple, a scholar, a general, an imperial in-law and a singer of indeterminate sex, which is the point: the group is meant to include every kind of person.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Below them, the gods people actually pray to

hierarchy.title: The Gods of Daily Life
hierarchy.blurb: The deities of the household, the shop, the harbour and the village street. Several were mortals - a general, a fisherman's daughter, a failed examination candidate - promoted after death by decree.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: And at the edges: beasts that announce good government, and what breaks it

hierarchy.title: Beasts and Demons
hierarchy.blurb: The qilin and the fenghuang appear only under a just ruler, so their arrival is a political statement. The demons are what the New Year, the doorway and the pilgrimage road are defended against.

entities.name: Pangu
entities.role: The first being, who separated heaven from earth
epithets: He Who Held Apart the Sky
domains: the separation of heaven and earth
the body that became the world
entities.abode: Inside the egg, then between earth and sky
entities.bio: He broke out of the cosmic egg and held heaven and earth apart for eighteen thousand years until he died and became the world.
entities.longBio: The universe begins as an egg of undifferentiated chaos in which Pangu sleeps for eighteen thousand years. He wakes, breaks out, and the light clear part rises to become heaven while the heavy turbid part sinks to become earth - the yin and yang separating. Fearing they will close again he stands between them, growing ten feet a day, pushing them apart for another eighteen thousand years until they are fixed. Then, exhausted, he dies, and his body becomes the world: his breath the wind and clouds, his voice thunder, his left eye the sun and right eye the moon, his limbs the mountains, his blood the rivers, his flesh the soil, his hair the stars, his sweat the rain, and the parasites on his body the human race.
entities.variantTraditions: Pangu is not attested before the third century CE, far later than the sage-king traditions, and may be a southern or borrowed story that was fitted to the front of an existing system.

entities.name: Nuwa
entities.role: Creator of humankind, who repaired the broken sky
entities.abode: The world she repaired
entities.bio: She made people out of yellow clay and later melted stones of five colours to patch a hole in the sky.
entities.longBio: Nuwa has a woman's upper body and a serpent's or dragon's lower body. Finding the world empty she moulded people from yellow river clay, one at a time and carefully; growing tired, she dipped a cord in the mud and flicked it, and the spatters became people too - the tradition adds, uncomfortably, that the hand-made ones became the nobility and the flicked ones the common people. Her greater act comes later. When the water god Gonggong smashes his head against Mount Buzhou, the pillar of heaven, the sky cracks, fire and flood pour through and beasts devour the people. Nuwa smelts stones of five colours to patch the sky, cuts the legs off a giant turtle to prop up its four corners, kills the black dragon, and dams the flood with reed ash.
entities.variantTraditions: Nuwa is sometimes Fuxi's sister, sometimes his wife, and often both; Han dynasty tomb art shows the two with their serpent tails intertwined.

entities.name: Fuxi
entities.role: Giver of the trigrams, of writing, fishing and marriage
entities.abode: The Yellow River valley
entities.bio: The culture hero who saw the trigrams on a dragon-horse's back and gave people writing, nets and marriage.
entities.longBio: Fuxi is the first of the Three Sovereigns and the archetypal culture hero. Watching a dragon-horse emerge from the Yellow River with markings on its back, he devises the eight trigrams - the ba gua, sets of three broken and unbroken lines that became the basis of the Yijing and of an entire tradition of divination and cosmology. He is credited with replacing knotted cords with written characters, with teaching people to fish with nets and to hunt with weapons, with domesticating animals, and with instituting marriage so that families rather than clans became the unit of society. With Nuwa, his sister or wife or both, he repopulates the world after a flood. Han tomb reliefs show the pair with intertwined serpent tails, he holding a carpenter's square and she a compass.
entities.variantTraditions: The Fuxi of the classics is a culture hero rather than a god, and his elevation to a divine Sovereign belongs to later systematising.

entities.name: Gonggong
entities.role: The water god who broke the pillar of heaven
entities.abode: The waters
entities.bio: Defeated in a struggle for supremacy, he rammed the mountain that held up the sky and tilted the world.
entities.longBio: Gonggong is a water deity with a human head, red hair and a serpent's body, and he loses a fight - variously against Zhurong the fire god, against Zhuanxu, or against Yao's forces, depending on which text you read. In rage and shame he smashes his head into Mount Buzhou, the pillar supporting the northwest corner of the sky. The pillar breaks. The sky tilts down toward the northwest, which is why the sun, moon and stars move in that direction, and the earth tilts down toward the southeast, which is why all the rivers of China flow that way to the sea. This is one of the more satisfying pieces of aetiology in any mythology: a losing tantrum explains the entire observed geography and astronomy of a continent.
entities.variantTraditions: Whom Gonggong fought differs across the Huainanzi, the Liezi and later sources, and the flood he causes is sometimes merged with the flood Yu the Great later controls.

entities.name: Zhurong
entities.role: God of fire
entities.abode: The south
entities.bio: The fire god who defeated Gonggong, and in one account executed Gun for failing to stop the flood.
entities.longBio: Zhurong governs fire and the southern quarter, and Chinese cosmology's five-phase system makes that a real office rather than a metaphor: south, summer, red and fire are one set, and he directs it. His best-known act is defeating Gonggong in the struggle that ends with the pillar of heaven broken - so the fire god's victory is what tilts the world. In the flood narratives he appears again as the executioner sent to kill Gun, Yu the Great's father, for stealing heaven's self-expanding soil, and it is from Gun's opened body that Yu is born. He is credited in some texts with teaching the use of fire. The name also belongs to a hereditary office of fire-master in the historical record, which blurs god and official in a way that is characteristic of this material.
entities.variantTraditions: Zhurong is variously a god, an official title and an ancestor of southern clans; the Chuci and the Shanhaijing treat him differently.

entities.name: Xihe
entities.role: Mother of the ten suns
entities.abode: Beyond the eastern sea, at the Fusang tree
entities.bio: She bore ten suns, bathed them in the eastern pool, and drove one across the sky each day in turn.
entities.longBio: Xihe lives beyond the eastern sea where the giant mulberry Fusang grows, and she is the mother of ten suns, each a three-legged crow. The arrangement is orderly: she washes them in the pool of Ganyuan, and each day one climbs the mulberry and is carried across the sky in her chariot drawn by six dragons while the other nine wait in the branches. It works until the ten decide to come out together, and the earth begins to burn - which is the crisis Houyi is sent to solve. Her counterpart Changxi bears the twelve moons and performs the same office for them. In some readings Xihe is not a mother at all but an official title for the astronomers who regulated the calendar, and the Shujing uses the name that way.
entities.variantTraditions: The Shujing's Xi and He are court astronomers, not a goddess; whether the deity or the office came first is unresolved.

entities.name: The Yellow Emperor
entities.role: Founder of Chinese civilisation and patron of Daoism
entities.abode: Mount Kunlun, and afterwards heaven
entities.bio: The archetypal ruler: he defeated Chiyou, ordered the state, and rose to heaven on a dragon.
entities.longBio: The Yellow Emperor is where Chinese myth and Chinese history are deliberately spliced together. He defeats the metal-bodied Chiyou at Zhuolu, using a south-pointing chariot to find his way through the fog Chiyou raises, and unites the tribes of the Yellow River plain. To him are credited, variously, the calendar, the compass, boats, carts, coined money, the first medical text, the standardisation of writing, and the invention of silk by his wife Leizu. At the end he casts a great bronze tripod, and when it is finished a dragon comes down to fetch him and he ascends to heaven with his court, some seventy people, holding onto its whiskers. Daoists later claimed him as a founder, and the medical classic that bears his name is still consulted.
entities.variantTraditions: The Yellow Emperor was treated as literal history for most of Chinese tradition and given precise dates; modern scholarship treats him as legendary.

entities.name: Shennong
entities.role: The Divine Farmer, who tasted every herb
entities.abode: The southern plains
entities.bio: He invented the plough and tested hundreds of herbs on himself, and was finally killed by one of them.
entities.longBio: Shennong taught people to farm - the plough, the axe, irrigation, the preservation of seed, the calendar of planting - and to hold markets, which the tradition regards as an equally important invention. His other work was medical and personally hazardous: he tasted hundreds of plants to determine which cured, which poisoned and which did neither, and in the most vivid version he had a transparent abdomen so he could watch what each did as it passed through him. He is said to have poisoned himself seventy times in one day and cured himself each time with tea, and finally to have eaten a yellow flower with a lethal effect he could not counter, and died of it. The pharmacopoeia bearing his name remained the foundation of Chinese herbal medicine for two thousand years.
entities.variantTraditions: Shennong and Yandi the Flame Emperor are identified in some sources and distinguished in others; the merger appears to be later.

entities.name: Chiyou
entities.role: The metal-headed rebel defeated at Zhuolu
symbols: a bronze head with an iron forehead
entities.abode: Zhuolu, and afterwards the standards of armies
entities.bio: A horned, metal-bodied war leader with eighty-one brothers, defeated by the Yellow Emperor and afterwards worshipped as a god of war.
entities.longBio: Chiyou has a bronze head and an iron forehead, horns, and eighty-one brothers each with the same, and he is credited with the invention of metal weapons - which is why he can fight the Yellow Emperor at all. At Zhuolu he raises a fog so thick the imperial army cannot move, and is defeated only when Huangdi builds the south-pointing chariot to navigate it, and with help variously from the drought spirit Nuba, the dragon Yinglong and a war drum made from the hide of a one-legged beast. Chiyou is executed, and his fetters thrown away become a maple wood that runs red. Then the characteristic turn: the Yellow Emperor has his image painted on banners to frighten enemies, and Chiyou becomes a god of war worshipped by later armies, including Han imperial ones.
entities.variantTraditions: Chiyou is claimed as an ancestor by the Miao and Hmong peoples, for whom the story reads very differently than in the Han imperial version.

entities.name: Yao
entities.role: The model emperor who passed over his own son
domains: the choosing of a successor by merit
entities.abode: Pingyang
entities.bio: The exemplary ruler of Confucian tradition, who gave the throne to a commoner rather than his son.
entities.longBio: Yao is the standard against which every later Chinese ruler is measured, and the reason is a single decision. Having a son he considered unworthy, he searched the empire for a successor and settled on Shun, a commoner of exemplary filial piety who had endured a murderous father, a spiteful stepmother and a treacherous half-brother without resentment. Yao tested him for years, gave him his two daughters in marriage to observe his household, and finally handed him the empire. This abdication in favour of merit rather than blood became the founding Confucian argument that legitimacy rests on virtue - and the founding awkwardness for every hereditary dynasty afterwards. His reign is also when the ten suns rise together and Houyi is sent to shoot them, and when the great flood begins.
entities.variantTraditions: The Shujing presents Yao as history. The abdication tradition was already contested in antiquity, and other early texts hint at a less voluntary transfer.

entities.name: Shun
entities.role: The commoner raised to the throne for his filial piety
entities.abode: Puban
entities.bio: Chosen by Yao for enduring a family that repeatedly tried to kill him without ceasing to honour them.
entities.longBio: Shun's father was blind and hostile, his stepmother malicious and his half-brother Xiang eager to inherit, and between them they tried to kill him more than once - sending him to repair a granary roof and setting it alight, sending him to dig a well and filling it in. He escaped both times, and continued to serve his father and treat his brother with courtesy, which is the entire point of the story: Confucian filial piety is not conditional on the parent deserving it. Yao heard of him, tested him, married his daughters to him, and gave him the empire. As emperor Shun organised the administration into departments, standardised weights and measures and the calendar, appointed Yu to control the flood, and in his turn passed the throne to Yu rather than to his own son.
entities.variantTraditions: The Mencius and the Shujing dwell on the family cruelty at length; later commentators found the willingness to keep honouring such a father genuinely difficult.

entities.name: Yu the Great
entities.role: Who controlled the flood by digging channels
domains: the division of the land into nine provinces
entities.abode: The nine provinces he surveyed
entities.bio: He worked thirteen years dredging channels to the sea, passing his own door three times without going in.
entities.longBio: Yu's father Gun tried to dam the great flood with stolen self-expanding soil from heaven, failed, and was executed; Yu was born from his opened body and inherited the task. He changed the method entirely - instead of damming he dredged, cutting channels to lead the water to the sea, which is both an engineering principle and a political one that Chinese writers have quoted at rulers ever since. He worked thirteen years, aided in some accounts by a yellow dragon and a black turtle, and passed the door of his own house three times without going in, once hearing his newborn son cry, because the work was not finished. He walked with a limp afterwards from the labour. He divided the land into nine provinces, cast nine bronze cauldrons to represent them, and founded the Xia dynasty.
entities.variantTraditions: The Xia's historicity is debated; Yu's flood-control narrative is the foundation text of Chinese hydraulic statecraft regardless of whether he existed.

entities.name: Houyi
entities.role: The archer who shot down nine suns
domains: the elixir of immortality he lost
symbols: the red bow and white arrows
entities.abode: Earth, after being expelled from heaven
entities.bio: He shot nine of the ten suns out of the sky, was rewarded with an elixir of immortality, and lost it to his wife.
entities.longBio: When the ten suns come out together the crops burn, the rivers dry and the people begin to die, and Houyi is sent down with a red bow and white arrows. He shoots nine of them out of the sky - each falls as a three-legged crow - and leaves one, which is the sun we have. He also kills a series of monsters plaguing the land. The reward is complicated: in most versions heaven is angry that he killed the suns, who were the sun-god's children, and he and his wife Chang'e are made mortal and left on earth, so he seeks an elixir of immortality from the Queen Mother of the West and obtains a dose for two, or one to share. Chang'e takes it all and floats to the moon. His end is grim in most tellings - killed by a treacherous student with a club of peachwood.
entities.variantTraditions: Houyi the archer and Yi the later Xia usurper are conflated in some sources and separated in others; the elixir story has at least four incompatible motives for Chang'e.

entities.name: Chang'e
entities.role: The woman who flew to the moon
entities.abode: The Guang Han palace on the moon
festivals: The Mid-Autumn Festival, on the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month
entities.worship: Honoured at the Mid-Autumn Festival with mooncakes, lanterns and offerings of fruit set out under the full moon.
entities.bio: She swallowed her husband's elixir of immortality and rose to the moon, where she lives with a rabbit and a woodcutter.
entities.longBio: Chang'e drinks the elixir Houyi obtained from the Queen Mother of the West, and the accounts cannot agree why: she was greedy; she was preventing a thief from taking it while Houyi was away; she was preventing Houyi from becoming an immortal tyrant; she took it by accident. She becomes weightless and rises, and stops at the moon rather than continuing to heaven - in the kindest version, so as to stay as near her husband as she can. There she lives in a cold palace with a jade rabbit that pounds the elixir of immortality in a mortar, and with Wu Gang, a man condemned to cut an osmanthus tree that heals itself with every stroke. Her festival is the Mid-Autumn, when families eat mooncakes and look at the full moon together, which gives the story a warmth its details do not.
entities.variantTraditions: The moral colouring of Chang'e swings completely between sources - thief, protector, or victim - and Werner's telling is notably harsher than the popular festival version.

entities.name: The Jade Emperor
entities.role: Sovereign of the celestial bureaucracy
domains: the appointment and demotion of gods
symbols: the flat-topped imperial crown with hanging beads
entities.abode: The Palace of Purple Tenuity in the highest heaven
festivals: The Jade Emperor's birthday, ninth day of the first lunar month
entities.worship: Central to Daoist and folk religion. Offerings of sugarcane and elaborate paper memorials are burned to him at New Year, and petitions to lesser gods are understood to pass up through his bureaucracy.
entities.bio: Emperor of heaven, who governs gods and men through a civil service exactly like the imperial one.
entities.longBio: The Jade Emperor sits at the top of a celestial administration modelled precisely on the Chinese state: ministries, ranks, reports, audits, promotions and demotions. Gods hold posts and can be reassigned; the kitchen god files an annual report on each household; the god of a locality has jurisdiction like a magistrate. He is not a creator - the world exists before him - and his authority is administrative rather than absolute. His most famous administrative failure is Sun Wukong, whom he tries to neutralise by giving him the meaningless post of Keeper of the Heavenly Horses, then a sinecure guarding the peach garden, both of which backfire spectacularly and require the Buddha to intervene. His birthday is celebrated on the ninth day of the first lunar month.
entities.variantTraditions: The Jade Emperor rises to supremacy relatively late, promoted during the Song dynasty with imperial backing, and displaced earlier high gods such as Shangdi and Taiyi.

entities.name: The Queen Mother of the West
entities.role: Keeper of the peaches of immortality
epithets: Golden Mother of the Jade Pool
domains: the peaches that ripen once in three thousand years
symbols: the tiger's teeth and leopard's tail in her oldest form
entities.abode: Mount Kunlun, by the Jade Pool
entities.worship: A major Daoist deity, invoked for longevity. Her peach imagery is standard on birthday gifts for the elderly.
entities.bio: She keeps the orchard whose peaches confer immortality, and her transformation from monster to empress is the clearest case of a Chinese deity being rewritten.
entities.longBio: In the Shanhaijing, the earliest source, Xiwangmu has a human form with tiger's teeth and a leopard's tail, dishevelled hair and a jade headdress, and she presides over plague and punishment - a fearsome mountain power. Over the following centuries she is comprehensively rewritten into a beautiful and gracious empress of the immortals, keeper of an orchard on Kunlun whose peaches ripen once in three thousand years and confer immortality on whoever eats one. She grants the elixir to Houyi and receives King Mu of Zhou as a guest. In Journey to the West her peach banquet is the occasion of Sun Wukong's greatest outrage. The distance between the two versions is one of the most instructive things in Chinese religion: it shows a goddess being promoted.
entities.variantTraditions: The Shanhaijing Xiwangmu and the Daoist empress are effectively different beings; a second-century BCE popular movement in her name also swept several provinces.

entities.name: Leigong and Dianmu
entities.role: The Duke of Thunder and the Mother of Lightning
domains: the punishment of secret crimes and undutiful children
symbols: the beaked face and bat wings
entities.abode: The Ministry of Thunder
entities.bio: A blue, winged, beaked god who beats thunder-drums, with his wife flashing mirrors to show him his target.
entities.longBio: Leigong has a blue body, wings, claws and a beaked face, and carries a mallet and a string of drums which he beats to make thunder. His wife Dianmu holds a mirror in each hand and flashes lightning to illuminate the target, because Leigong is understood to strike people and must be shown who. Their department punishes crimes that human justice has missed - secret murders, undutiful children, the adulteration of goods, the wasting of grain - which makes them the enforcement arm of a moral order that assumes most wrongdoing goes undetected. Being struck by lightning was accordingly read as evidence of concealed guilt. They belong to a Ministry of Thunder with a full staff including gods of wind, rain and clouds, which is the celestial bureaucracy working exactly as advertised.
entities.variantTraditions: Leigong appears in many local variants and folk stories, often as a figure who can be tricked or trapped by a clever farmer.

entities.name: The Dragon Kings
entities.role: Four brothers who govern the seas and the rain
epithets: Ao Guang of the Eastern Sea
domains: the granting or withholding of water
entities.abode: Crystal palaces beneath the four seas
entities.worship: Dragon king temples stood beside rivers and coasts everywhere. Rain processions and petitions were a normal part of village life in drought.
entities.bio: Dragon kings hold the rain as an office: they can be petitioned, and they can be reported for failing to deliver.
entities.longBio: The Dragon Kings are the clearest illustration of the bureaucratic principle. Four brothers rule the four seas, with lesser dragon kings in every river, lake and well, and their job is to deliver rain on the schedule the Jade Emperor's ministry sets. Villages petitioned them in drought; if petitioning failed, communities were quite prepared to carry the dragon king's statue out into the sun to let him feel the drought himself, or to lodge a formal complaint. One famous story has a dragon king executed for altering the amount of rain in his orders by a few drops. Ao Guang of the Eastern Sea appears in Journey to the West, bullied out of the iron pillar that becomes Sun Wukong's staff, and in the Nezha story, where his son is killed and skinned.
entities.variantTraditions: The Dragon Kings owe a good deal to the Buddhist naga kings imported with Indian texts, layered onto older indigenous water deities.

entities.name: Yanluo Wang
entities.role: Judge of the dead and lord of the first court of hell
entities.abode: Diyu, the courts beneath the earth
entities.bio: He examines the record of each life, assigns punishment by department, and sends the soul back to be reborn.
entities.longBio: Yanluo Wang is a Chinese official who happens to run hell. Diyu is organised as ten courts, each under a king, each handling particular offences with a specialised department, and souls are processed through them in sequence - examined against a written record of their deeds, sentenced, punished for a fixed term, and then sent to the Wheel of Rebirth. It is not eternal and it is not arbitrary; it is a legal system with paperwork, and stories abound of clerical errors, of the wrong person summoned by a mistake in the register and sent back, and of bribes attempted. Yanluo derives from the Indian Yama, imported with Buddhism, and was fitted into an existing Chinese apparatus of underworld administration.
entities.variantTraditions: The ten-court scheme is a medieval Chinese elaboration; the Indian Yama who lies behind Yanluo is a rather different figure, as the Hindu pack shows.

entities.name: The Kitchen God
entities.role: Who watches the household and reports annually
symbols: the paper image above the stove
entities.abode: Above the stove, in every kitchen
festivals: The send-off of the Kitchen God, around the twenty-third day of the twelfth lunar month
entities.worship: Among the most universally observed domestic rites in China: nearly every household kept an image and performed the annual send-off.
entities.bio: His paper image watches the family all year, then goes up in smoke to report on them at New Year.
entities.longBio: The Kitchen God's image is pasted above the stove, and he observes everything the household says and does. Shortly before the lunar New Year he ascends to report to the Jade Emperor, and the family's fortunes for the coming year depend on what he says. The response is beautifully pragmatic: they smear his mouth with malt sugar or honey so that his lips stick together and he can only say sweet things, then burn the image so he rises with the smoke, and paste up a fresh one when he returns. His origin story is that of a man who abandoned his wife, fell into poverty, and unknowingly begged at her door; recognising her, he threw himself into the hearth in shame, and she made him a god of it.
entities.variantTraditions: Local versions of his origin differ widely, and the sugaring of the mouth is attested across most of China with regional variations in the sweet used.

entities.name: Zhongli Quan
entities.role: Eldest of the Eight Immortals; bearer of the reviving fan
entities.abode: Mount Zhongnan
entities.bio: A Han general who found the elixir in a cave wall and whose fan revives the dead.
entities.longBio: Zhongli Quan is shown as a stout, cheerful, bare-bellied man with a feather fan, and the fan is his instrument: he waves it and the dead come back. The story is that he was a Han dynasty general who lost a battle, fled into the mountains, and was taught by a Daoist master; later an earthquake or a cracked wall revealed a jade casket with instructions for the elixir of immortality. He is credited with the power to turn base metal into silver, which he used to relieve famines. He recruits Lu Dongbin, the most famous of the Eight, by putting him through a long series of dream-tests. As eldest of the group he generally leads it.
entities.variantTraditions: The Eight Immortals as a fixed set of eight are a Yuan and Ming dynasty crystallisation; earlier lists differ in membership.

entities.name: Lu Dongbin
entities.role: Scholar-swordsman, most famous of the Eight Immortals
symbols: the sword slung on the back
entities.abode: Mount Zhongnan, and wherever he wanders in disguise
entities.bio: A failed scholar shown his whole future life in a dream while millet cooked, who woke and left to seek the Way.
entities.longBio: Lu Dongbin fails the imperial examinations repeatedly, and in an inn meets Zhongli Quan, who sets millet cooking and lends him a pillow. He dreams an entire successful life: examinations passed, high office, wealth, a large family, then slander, disgrace, exile, the death of his children, and destitution in old age. He wakes; the millet is not yet done. He leaves with Zhongli Quan. He carries a sword said to subdue demons, wanders in disguise testing people's virtue, and is a patron of scholars, barbers and the sick. He is by far the most popular of the Eight in folk religion, with a great many temples, and is credited with a large body of Daoist internal alchemy writing.
entities.variantTraditions: The millet dream is one of the most retold stories in Chinese literature and appears in several versions with different dreamers.

entities.name: Li Tieguai
entities.role: Iron-crutch Li, who came back to the wrong body
domains: the relief of the poor and sick
entities.abode: Wherever the sick and poor are
entities.bio: His spirit left his body to visit heaven; his disciple burned the body, and he woke in a dead beggar's corpse.
entities.longBio: Li was a handsome and accomplished adept who could send his spirit out of his body. Leaving to visit Laozi on Mount Hua, he told his disciple to guard the body for seven days and burn it if he had not returned. On the sixth day the disciple's mother fell mortally ill; he burned the body and left. Li's spirit returned to find nothing to enter but the fresh corpse of a lame beggar who had starved by the roadside, and he has been in it ever since - dirty, crippled, leaning on an iron crutch. Laozi gave him a gourd of medicine. The moral the tradition draws is straightforward and repeated everywhere: he is the reminder that the form is not the person.
entities.variantTraditions: Some tellings excuse the disciple entirely and others blame him; the burning is variously six days or the seventh morning.

entities.name: He Xiangu
entities.role: The one woman among the Eight Immortals
entities.abode: Mount Luofu
entities.bio: She ate a supernatural stone as a girl, stopped needing food, and refused marriage to pursue the Way.
entities.longBio: He Xiangu is the only woman consistently counted among the Eight. As a girl she dreamed, or met, a spirit who told her to eat powdered mica or a stone of a particular kind; having done so she became weightless, ceased to need ordinary food, and could move over hills at great speed. She refused marriage, lived on wild herbs, and gathered fruit in the mountains for her mother. Summoned to court by the Empress Wu, she disappeared on the way. She carries a lotus, which stands for purity emerging unstained from mud, and she is invoked in domestic matters and by unmarried women. The presence of one woman among eight is often read as deliberate: the group is meant to include every kind of person.
entities.variantTraditions: Her identity is unstable across sources - several different historical or legendary women named He are proposed as the original.

entities.name: Zhang Guolao
entities.role: The old man who rode his donkey backwards
entities.abode: Mount Zhongtiao
entities.bio: He rode a white donkey backwards, folded it like paper when not in use, and dodged imperial summons by dying.
entities.longBio: Zhang Guolao is the eccentric of the group and is based on a historical Tang dynasty recluse. He travelled thousands of miles a day on a white donkey which he folded up like a sheet of paper and put in his wallet when he arrived, sprinkling water on it to restore it. He rode it backwards, on the principle - the tradition says - that all things go backwards. Summoned repeatedly by Tang emperors he refused, and when finally compelled he dropped dead at the palace gate and rotted; the messengers turned back, and he was seen alive again shortly after. He carries a bamboo drum and is invoked by couples wanting children.
entities.variantTraditions: Zhang Guo is attested in the Tang histories as a real recluse who refused imperial summonses; the donkey is the legendary accretion.

entities.name: Han Xiangzi
entities.role: The flute player who made flowers open
domains: the forcing of flowers out of season
entities.abode: Mount Zhongnan
entities.bio: Nephew of the great Confucian Han Yu, whose flute made things grow and who foretold his uncle's exile.
entities.longBio: Han Xiangzi is presented as the nephew of Han Yu, the famous Tang statesman and Confucian polemicist who wrote a celebrated memorial against Buddhism and was exiled for it. The pairing is pointed: the arch-Confucian has a Daoist immortal in the family, and the stories play the contrast for all it is worth. Han Xiangzi plays a flute whose music makes plants grow and flowers open out of season, and at a family gathering he causes a peony to bloom bearing a couplet on its petals prophesying his uncle's exile to the far south, which the uncle dismisses and which then happens exactly. He is patron of musicians and is shown with a flute and a basket of flowers.
entities.variantTraditions: The historical Han Yu did have a great-nephew named Han Xiang; the immortal is a legendary elaboration on him.

entities.name: Cao Guojiu
entities.role: The imperial relative who left the court in shame
entities.abode: The mountains, after the court
entities.bio: Brother of an empress, he withdrew into the mountains after his own brother's crimes shamed him.
entities.longBio: Cao Guojiu was the brother of a Song empress, and his younger brother used the family connection to commit crimes including murder and escape punishment. Cao was so ashamed of the family's conduct that he gave away his property and withdrew to the mountains to study the Way. Zhongli Quan and Lu Dongbin found him there and asked what he was cultivating; he said the Way; they asked where the Way was, and he pointed at the sky; they asked where the sky was, and he pointed at his heart, and they accepted him. He carries the jade tablet an official holds at court, and he is patron of actors and of the theatre, which is a curious fate for a man who left public life to avoid being looked at.
entities.variantTraditions: The historical identification with a Song imperial in-law is uncertain, and the crimes attributed to his brother vary.

entities.name: Lan Caihe
entities.role: The ragged singer whose sex is never settled
entities.abode: The streets and markets
entities.bio: A wandering singer in rags, one foot bare, who scattered the coins given and finally rose from a tavern on a crane.
entities.longBio: Lan Caihe wanders the towns in a tattered blue gown with a belt of black wood, wearing a boot on one foot and nothing on the other, in a padded coat in summer and thin clothes in the snow, singing verses that mock the pursuit of wealth. Coins given are strung on a cord and either scattered for the poor or simply dragged along the ground and left. The sources are conspicuously unsettled about whether Lan Caihe is a man, a woman, or neither, and the ambiguity appears to be deliberate rather than a gap in the record. The end is the standard immortal's exit: in a tavern, hearing music from the air, rising on a crane and dropping gown, belt and one boot back to the ground.
entities.variantTraditions: Lan Caihe's sex is left indeterminate in the earliest accounts and settled differently by later artists; opera traditionally casts the role young and androgynous.

entities.name: Sun Wukong
entities.role: The Monkey King, who fought heaven and lost to a hand
entities.abode: The Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, and the road west
entities.bio: Born from a stone, he mastered every art, wrecked heaven's banquet, and was pinned under a mountain for five hundred years.
entities.longBio: Sun Wukong is born from a stone egg on a mountain, becomes king of the monkeys, and sets out to defeat death - learning the seventy-two transformations and the cloud-somersault that crosses thirty-six thousand miles. He erases his name from the ledgers of hell, bullies the Dragon King out of an iron pillar that becomes his staff, and is bought off by heaven with the meaningless post of Keeper of the Heavenly Horses. Discovering the insult he rebels, is given the empty title Great Sage Equal to Heaven, eats the peaches of immortality, wrecks the Queen Mother's banquet, and defeats every army sent against him. The Buddha ends it with a wager: leap out of my palm. He somersaults to the end of the universe, marks a pillar, and finds he has not left the Buddha's hand.
entities.variantTraditions: Journey to the West is a sixteenth-century novel built on much older pilgrimage legend; Sun Wukong's possible relation to Hanuman has been argued for a century without resolution.

entities.name: Tang Sanzang
entities.role: The monk who walked to India for the scriptures
entities.abode: The road from Chang'an to India
entities.bio: A gentle, fearful, incorruptible monk whose flesh grants immortality, escorted west by three converted monsters.
entities.longBio: Tang Sanzang is based on the real seventh-century monk Xuanzang, who genuinely walked to India and back and brought home a library of Buddhist texts. The novel makes him almost helpless: he cannot fight, he weeps easily, he is repeatedly deceived, and he is frequently captured because every demon on the route knows that eating his flesh confers immortality. His virtue is real but frustrating - he cannot tell a disguised demon from a human, and he punishes Sun Wukong for killing them, tightening the golden headband with a chant until the monkey rolls on the ground. The tension between his compassion and Wukong's competence is the engine of the whole book.
entities.variantTraditions: The historical Xuanzang's own travel record is a sober and invaluable geographical document; the novel's Tripitaka is almost its opposite in temperament.

entities.name: Zhu Bajie
entities.role: Pigsy, the marshal of heaven demoted into a pig's body
entities.abode: Gao Village, and the road west
entities.bio: Once a heavenly marshal, banished for drunkenly harassing the moon goddess and reborn in a pig's womb.
entities.longBio: Zhu Bajie was Marshal Tianpeng, commander of a hundred thousand of heaven's naval forces, until he got drunk at a banquet and made advances to Chang'e. He was banished to earth, and the reincarnation went wrong - he entered a sow's womb and came out as a pig-man. He is greedy, lazy, cowardly, permanently hungry and permanently interested in women, and he repeatedly suggests the pilgrimage be abandoned and the party sell the horse and go home. He is also genuinely brave when cornered, fights well with a nine-toothed rake, and never actually leaves. The novel uses him for comedy and then quietly refuses to discard him, which is a large part of why readers are fond of him.
entities.variantTraditions: His name means Eight Precepts, the monastic vows he is supposed to keep and conspicuously does not.

entities.name: Sha Wujing
entities.role: Sandy, the river ogre who carries the luggage
entities.abode: The Flowing Sands River, and the road west
entities.bio: A heavenly general banished for breaking a cup, who ate travellers at a river until he was recruited.
entities.longBio: Sha Wujing was the Curtain-Raising General in the celestial court, and his crime was to break a crystal cup at the Queen Mother's banquet. For that he was flogged, exiled, and condemned to have a flying sword pierce his chest a hundred times a day. He took up residence in the Flowing Sands River and ate travellers, wearing the skulls of nine previous pilgrims - who turn out to be Tang Sanzang's own earlier incarnations - around his neck. Converted by Guanyin, he becomes the steadiest and least troublesome of the three disciples: he says little, does not quarrel, carries the baggage, and is the one who reliably stays when the others are storming off. The severity of the punishment against the triviality of the offence is the point.
entities.variantTraditions: Sha Wujing has the least developed characterisation of the four and is often given more to do in adaptations than in the novel.

entities.name: Guanyin
entities.role: Bodhisattva of compassion, who hears the cries of the world
epithets: She Who Hears the Cries of the World
entities.abode: Mount Putuo
festivals: Guanyin's birthday, nineteenth day of the second lunar month
entities.worship: The most widely worshipped deity in Chinese religion, present in Buddhist temples, Daoist temples and private homes alike. Mount Putuo is her pilgrimage island.
entities.bio: The most widely worshipped deity in China, who changed sex in transmission and refuses nirvana until all are saved.
entities.longBio: Guanyin is the Chinese form of the Indian bodhisattva Avalokitesvara, and the transformation is remarkable: male in India and in early Chinese Buddhism, and unambiguously female from around the Song dynasty onward, which is one of the best documented sex-changes of any deity anywhere. As a bodhisattva she has postponed her own final enlightenment until every being is saved. She hears whoever calls, and rescue stories attach to her by the thousand. In Journey to the West she is the one who assembles and supervises the pilgrimage. In folk religion she grants children, protects sailors and the sick, and is the deity most likely to be found on a household altar. Her thousand-armed, thousand-eyed form expresses the same idea as her name: she sees and reaches everywhere.
entities.variantTraditions: The legend of the princess Miaoshan, who is martyred by her father and returns to heal him with her own hands and eyes, is a Chinese story attached to her that has no Indian original.

entities.name: Nezha
entities.role: The child-god who gave his body back to his parents
entities.abode: Chentang Pass, and the celestial altar
entities.bio: He killed a dragon king's son, and when his father was threatened he returned his flesh and bones and was rebuilt from lotus.
entities.longBio: Nezha is born after a three-year pregnancy as a ball of flesh that his father strikes with a sword, releasing a boy who can already walk and speak. Playing in the sea he kills the Dragon King's son and pulls out his sinews, and the Dragon Kings threaten to flood the region and destroy his family in reprisal. Nezha's answer is the most extraordinary act in Chinese myth: to sever the debt of the body, he cuts out his own bones and flesh and returns them to his father and mother, so that nothing of theirs is destroyed with him. His master Taiyi Zhenren rebuilds him from lotus root and stalks, giving him a body that owes his parents nothing, and he becomes a fierce protective deity riding wind-fire wheels.
entities.variantTraditions: Nezha derives ultimately from a Buddhist protector figure of Indian origin, thoroughly reworked through Fengshen Yanyi and Journey to the West.

entities.name: Erlang Shen
entities.role: The three-eyed god who caught the Monkey King
symbols: the third eye on the forehead
entities.abode: Guankou, on the Min River
entities.bio: Nephew of the Jade Emperor and the only one able to match Sun Wukong transformation for transformation.
entities.longBio: Erlang Shen has a third eye in the middle of his forehead that sees through any disguise, which is exactly the ability the celestial armies lack when Sun Wukong rebels. Their duel in Journey to the West is one of the great set pieces: the two chase each other through form after form - sparrow, cormorant, fish, water-snake, bustard - each countering the other, until Wukong turns into a temple and cannot hide his tail, which he leaves standing behind as a flagpole. Erlang spots it. Wukong is finally brought down by Laozi's ring while distracted. Erlang is also identified with Li Bing's son and with the historical hydraulic engineering at Dujiangyan, so he is a flood-control god as well as a martial one.
entities.variantTraditions: Erlang's identity is a composite of at least three figures - Li Erlang, Yang Jian and a Sichuan hunting god - never fully reconciled.

entities.name: Guan Yu
entities.role: A Han general promoted to god of war and of loyalty
entities.abode: Temples in every Chinese community on earth
festivals: Guandi's birthday, twenty-fourth day of the sixth lunar month
entities.worship: Temples worldwide. Sworn brotherhoods, merchants, soldiers, police and triads all invoke him, each for the loyalty rather than the violence.
entities.bio: A real third-century general whose reputation for loyalty raised him, over a thousand years, to one of the greatest gods in China.
entities.longBio: Guan Yu was an actual general of the Three Kingdoms period who died in 220 CE, and his afterlife is the clearest possible demonstration of how the Chinese pantheon works. His reputation for absolute loyalty to his sworn brother Liu Bei - he refuses enormous inducements to change sides, and returns to a losing cause - made him first a local ghost, then a Buddhist protector, then a Daoist deity, then a Ming emperor's official god of war, and finally an object of imperial sacrifice on a level with Confucius. Merchants worship him for the same quality applied to contracts; so, notoriously, do police and criminal societies alike, both prizing loyalty. A mortal did not become a god by ascending. He was promoted, repeatedly, by decree.
entities.variantTraditions: Guan Yu's canonisation is documented in imperial edicts across several dynasties, which makes him unusually traceable: the paperwork of a deification survives.

entities.name: Mazu
entities.role: Goddess of the sea and protector of sailors
domains: the protection of fishermen and sailors
entities.abode: Meizhou Island, and every port
festivals: Mazu's birthday, twenty-third day of the third lunar month
entities.worship: Thousands of temples across the Chinese-speaking world. Her Meizhou pilgrimage and the Dajia procession in Taiwan draw enormous crowds.
entities.bio: A Fujianese fisherman's daughter who died young saving sailors, and became the sea goddess of the whole Chinese diaspora.
entities.longBio: Mazu was Lin Moniang, born on Meizhou Island in the tenth century, a girl who did not cry as an infant - hence her nickname, the silent girl - and who learned to swim, to predict weather and to rescue people from the sea. She died young, in most accounts while going out to save her father and brother in a storm. Fishermen began to report her appearing in storms as a light or a girl in red guiding them home, and her cult spread along the coast, out to Taiwan, and with emigrants to Southeast Asia and beyond, with successive dynasties elevating her title until she was Empress of Heaven. Her temples are the anchor institutions of overseas Chinese communities, and her procession is among the largest religious gatherings in the world.
entities.variantTraditions: Mazu's historicity is reasonably secure in outline; the accretion of miracle accounts and imperial titles is exceptionally well documented.

entities.name: Caishen
entities.role: God of wealth
entities.abode: The Ministry of Wealth
festivals: Welcoming the God of Wealth, fifth day of the first lunar month
entities.bio: Welcomed into every shop and household at New Year, and identified with several different historical or legendary men.
entities.longBio: Caishen is less a single figure than an office, and at least four candidates hold it depending on region and period - most commonly Zhao Gongming, a Fengshen Yanyi general who rides a black tiger and carries an iron whip, but also Bi Gan, a minister whose heart was cut out by a tyrant and who is therefore said to be perfectly impartial having no heart to be partial with. He is welcomed on the fifth day of the New Year with firecrackers and offerings, and his image hangs in shops. Some accounts split the office into civil and martial gods of wealth. His prominence says something plain about the religion: prosperity is a legitimate thing to petition heaven for, and nobody in the tradition finds that awkward.
entities.variantTraditions: The identification of Caishen varies so widely by region that any single biography is local rather than canonical.

entities.name: Zhong Kui
entities.role: The ugly scholar who became the queller of demons
entities.abode: The gates and doorways of houses
entities.worship: Images pasted at doorways at New Year and during the Dragon Boat Festival. Popular with examination candidates, for obvious reasons.
entities.bio: He took first place in the imperial examination, was denied it for his ugliness, killed himself, and was made king of ghosts.
entities.longBio: Zhong Kui passed the imperial examination at the top of the list, and the emperor - or the court - stripped him of the honour on account of his extreme ugliness. He killed himself on the palace steps. The emperor, appalled, had him buried with the honours of a high official, and in gratitude Zhong Kui's ghost undertook to hunt down and destroy demons. The tradition says the emperor Xuanzong later saw him in a fever dream catching a small demon that had been stealing from the palace, and on waking commissioned a painting of him from the court artist Wu Daozi. That painting established the image: a huge bearded man in official robes with a drawn sword. His picture is pasted on doors at New Year to keep evil out.
entities.variantTraditions: The Xuanzong dream story is the standard origin and is itself Tang or later; the character may derive from an older ritual object or a pun on a demon-expelling mallet.

entities.name: Tudigong
entities.role: The earth god of one small place
domains: a single village, field or street
the reporting of local affairs upward
entities.abode: A small shrine at the edge of the village or field
entities.worship: The most numerous shrines in China. Offerings on the first and fifteenth of each lunar month, and at planting and harvest.
entities.bio: The lowest-ranking god in the celestial civil service, with jurisdiction over one village and a duty to report upward.
entities.longBio: Tudigong is the bottom of the bureaucracy and by far its most present member. Every village, every field, sometimes every street has one, housed in a small shrine that may be no more than a niche of bricks, and he is depicted as a kindly old man with a white beard and a staff. His jurisdiction is tiny and his duties are exactly those of a local magistrate: he keeps order in his patch, receives petitions about immediate matters - a lost animal, a sick child, a boundary dispute - and reports what happens to his superiors. The dead are notified to him. He has no cosmic role whatever, which is the point: the system reaches all the way down, and the god you actually deal with is a neighbour with a small office.
entities.variantTraditions: Tudigong shrines vary enormously in form, and in some regions his wife Tudipo is included, in others deliberately not.

entities.name: Yue Lao
entities.role: The old man under the moon, who ties the red thread
epithets: The Old Man Under the Moon
entities.abode: Under the moon, wherever couples are fated
entities.worship: Shrines to Yue Lao within larger temples attract unmarried people leaving petitions; red cords are bought and tied as offerings.
entities.bio: He binds the ankles of destined couples with an invisible red cord that cannot be broken however far apart they live.
entities.longBio: Yue Lao sits under the moon reading a book of marriages and ties an invisible red cord around the ankles of two people who are fated to marry, and the tradition is firm that the cord may stretch and tangle but cannot break - the couple will marry regardless of distance, family opposition, wealth or their own preferences. The classic story has a young man meet him, ask about his own future wife, and be shown a poor three-year-old girl in a market; disgusted, he hires someone to stab her. Fourteen years later he marries a beautiful young woman who wears an ornament on her forehead, and asks why: it covers a scar from a knife, from when she was three. The image of the red thread is now common across East Asia.
entities.variantTraditions: The story appears in the ninth-century collection Xu Youguai Lu; the red thread motif spread to Japan and Korea and is now often assumed to be older than it is.

entities.name: The Weaver Girl and the Cowherd
entities.role: Lovers separated by the Milky Way, allowed one night a year
domains: the seventh night of the seventh month
entities.abode: Opposite banks of the Milky Way
festivals: Qixi, the seventh night of the seventh lunar month
entities.bio: A celestial weaver married a mortal herdsman; the Milky Way was drawn between them, and magpies bridge it once a year.
entities.longBio: Zhinu, a weaver of the clouds and a granddaughter of the Jade Emperor, comes down to bathe and the cowherd Niulang, advised by his ox, takes her clothes so she must stay. They marry and have two children. When heaven notices, she is taken back, and when Niulang pursues her - carrying the children in baskets, wearing the hide of his ox, who has died so that he can - the Queen Mother draws a hairpin across the sky and a river of stars appears between them. They stand on opposite banks. Once a year, on the seventh night of the seventh month, all the magpies in the world fly up and make a bridge with their wings, and the two cross to meet. Rain that night is said to be their tears.
entities.variantTraditions: The stars are Vega and Altair, genuinely separated by the Milky Way; the story is attested from the Han dynasty and has parallel versions in Japan, Korea and Vietnam.

entities.name: The Qilin
entities.role: The gentle beast that appears when a sage is born
entities.abode: Wherever a just ruler governs
entities.bio: It walks without bending the grass, appears at the birth or death of a sage, and will not harm anything living.
entities.longBio: The qilin has the body of a deer or horse, ox's hooves, scales, and a single fleshy horn, and its defining quality is that it will not tread on a living blade of grass or eat living vegetation. It appears only in the reign of a benevolent ruler or at the birth of a sage - one is said to have appeared to Confucius' mother before his birth, and the capture and killing of a qilin late in his life is recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals, where Confucius is said to have wept and stopped writing. Its appearance is therefore a political statement as much as a wonder. In the fifteenth century Zheng He's fleet brought a giraffe back from Africa and presented it at court as a qilin.
entities.variantTraditions: The giraffe presentation of 1414 is historical, and the Korean and Japanese words for giraffe still derive from qilin.

entities.name: The Fenghuang
entities.role: The bird of the south, wrongly called the Chinese phoenix
entities.abode: The Kunlun mountains, and the paulownia tree
entities.bio: It appears in times of peace, eats only bamboo seed, and is paired with the dragon as empress to emperor.
entities.longBio: The fenghuang is a composite bird - a pheasant's head, a swallow's beak, a tortoise's back, a fish's tail - with plumage of the five colours that correspond to the five virtues. It appears only in periods of peace and good government, nests only in the paulownia, drinks only from sweet springs and eats only bamboo seed. Paired with the dragon it stands for the empress against the emperor, and the two together are the standard motif for a marriage. It is habitually called the Chinese phoenix in English, which is misleading: it does not burn, does not die and does not rise from ashes, and its association with fire and rebirth is imported from a Mediterranean bird it has nothing to do with.
entities.variantTraditions: Originally feng was male and huang female, two birds; the compound became one bird and then a feminine symbol, which is a fairly drastic sex change of its own.

entities.name: The Four Symbols
entities.role: Azure Dragon, White Tiger, Vermilion Bird and Black Tortoise
symbols: the four creatures on tomb walls, banners and city gates
entities.abode: The four quarters of the sky
entities.bio: Four creatures governing the four directions, seasons and elements, and dividing the night sky between them.
entities.longBio: The Four Symbols are the primary organising scheme of Chinese cosmology and astronomy: the Azure Dragon holds the east, spring and wood; the Vermilion Bird the south, summer and fire; the White Tiger the west, autumn and metal; the Black Tortoise, entwined with a snake, the north, winter and water. The twenty-eight lunar mansions are divided seven to each. They appear on tomb walls to orient the dead, on city gates, on military banners and in the layout of capitals and graves, and they govern feng shui siting. Unlike most figures in this pack they are not really characters and have almost no stories; they are a coordinate system that happens to be alive.
entities.variantTraditions: The Yellow Dragon of the centre is sometimes added as a fifth, matching the five-phase scheme rather than the four directions.

entities.name: The Nian
entities.role: The beast that comes at the turn of the year
domains: the eating of livestock and children
fear of red, fire and noise
entities.abode: The mountains, or under the sea, until the year turns
festivals: Chinese New Year, whose red decorations and firecrackers are said to descend from driving it off
entities.bio: A beast that emerged once a year to devour villagers, and was driven off by red, noise and fire - which is why New Year looks the way it does.
entities.longBio: The nian lives hidden and comes out at the turn of the year to eat livestock, crops and people, particularly children. Villagers learned - from an old beggar in most versions - that it fears three things: the colour red, loud noise, and fire. So they paste red couplets on their doors, hang red lanterns, set off firecrackers and stay up through the night with the lights burning. That is a complete account of Chinese New Year decoration presented as a monster-defence procedure, and the word nian now simply means year. The story is a good example of a folk aetiology attached to a much older set of practices, explaining an existing festival rather than causing it.
entities.variantTraditions: The nian story is not attested in early sources and appears to be relatively modern, retrofitted to explain New Year customs of considerable antiquity.

entities.name: The Taotie
entities.role: The glutton mask on the bronzes
symbols: a face with huge eyes and no lower jaw
entities.abode: The surface of every Shang and Zhou bronze
entities.bio: A devouring face without a lower jaw, carved on ritual bronzes, later explained as a warning against greed.
entities.longBio: The taotie motif - a frontal animal face with enormous eyes, horns, and conspicuously no lower jaw - covers Shang and Zhou ritual bronzes, and it is one of the most recognisable images in Chinese art. The interpretation came much later than the object. Zhou and Han writers explained it as the taotie, a monster of gluttony that ate so much it consumed its own body and was left with only a head, and said it was placed on food vessels precisely as a warning against greed. Modern scholars are sceptical that the Shang bronzeworkers meant anything of the kind, and the original significance of the mask is genuinely unknown. It is a rare case of a myth demonstrably invented to explain an artefact nobody could read any more.
entities.variantTraditions: The name taotie is applied to the motif by Song antiquarians and later; whether the Shang had any such concept is unknown and probably unknowable.

entities.name: The White Bone Demon
entities.role: The skeleton spirit who fooled the pilgrim three times
epithets: The Lady of the White Bones
entities.abode: The mountains on the road west
entities.bio: She took three human forms to reach Tang Sanzang, and each time Sun Wukong killed her he was punished for it.
entities.longBio: The White Bone Demon wants to eat Tang Sanzang's flesh for the immortality it confers, and knows she cannot take him by force. So she appears three times in succession - as a young woman bringing food, then as an old woman searching for her missing daughter, then as an old man searching for both - and each time Sun Wukong sees through the disguise with his fiery eyes and kills her, and each time the corpse reverts to a human body and Tang Sanzang, seeing only murder, punishes him with the headband chant. After the third he expels Wukong from the pilgrimage altogether. It is the sharpest statement of the novel's central problem: the monk's compassion is genuine, and it is precisely what the demon uses.
entities.variantTraditions: The episode is among the most famous in the novel and is a staple of Chinese opera and film, usually played with more sympathy for Wukong than the text strictly gives.
